bullets: Textbook material: Material for biochemical testing and sample preparation; Centrifugation and electrophoresis; Chromatography; Optical methods: colorimetry, photometry, spectrophotometry
Practice: Q&A: 0 + 1

slides.title: Material for biochemical testing and sample preparation
bullets: The material is most often a biological fluid of the body or cell fractions; the qualitative and quantitative changes of the measured components, or the activity of enzymes taking part in the reaction, are compared in health and disease.
Plasma, serum and other biological fluids are watery mixtures of many natural substances.
When enzymes are measured, nothing that changes the composition is added to the fluid; if the enzyme concentration is high, the fluid is diluted.

If an enzyme in the fluid catalyses the substance being measured and interferes, its action is stopped with reagents such as trichloroacetic or phosphotungstic acid, or by heating; other proteins precipitate together with the enzyme.
To study components of cells or tissues, the tissue is first broken up mechanically in a homogeniser (in a medium that protects it).

slides.title: Material for biochemical testing and sample preparation
bullets: A homogenate is a complex mixture, so physico-chemical methods (centrifugation, electrophoresis, chromatography, optical methods) are used to separate it by molecules.

slides.title: Centrifugation and electrophoresis
bullets: Centrifugation separates the heavy parts of a fluid from the light ones by centrifugal force; heavier particles settle first, and the fluid above (supernatant) can be spun again faster to separate other fractions.

Preparative centrifugation is used to separate blood cells, to sediment cells in urine and for other purposes; clinical biochemistry laboratories use small-volume centrifuges, while high-speed ultracentrifuges serve to determine the molecular weight of proteins and nucleic acids (analytical centrifugation).
Differential centrifugation separates subcellular fractions — nuclei, mitochondria, lysosomes, microsomes; the settling speed grows with the centrifugal force (in units of g).
Electrophoresis is the distribution of charged particles under an external electric field; a modern method used in clinical medicine to analyse blood proteins and peptides, especially serum.

slides.title: Centrifugation and electrophoresis
bullets: Particles move at different speeds according to size and charge and separate; there are frontal and zonal types (zonal is more common); zonal carriers: filter paper, cellulose acetate, starch, agar, polyacrylamide gel (polyacrylamide-gel electrophoresis is now used most).
Fractions are stained with a dye (Coomassie blue, bromophenol blue, amido black); the intensity of staining is directly proportional to the amount of that protein.

slides.title: Chromatography
bullets: Chromatography studies how mixtures separate into their components; the lecture describes ion-exchange column, liquid and partition chromatography.

Ion-exchange column chromatography separates dissolved substances in ionic form: the stationary phase consists of ion-exchange resins (cation and anion exchangers); a substance with a larger charge interacts more strongly with the resin and moves more slowly down the column.
Substances held on the column are washed off with solutions of different pH; the liquid leaving the column — the eluate — is collected in a collector.
In liquid chromatography microscopic particles replace the stationary phase; the method is fast and separates almost any compound in a short time.

slides.title: Chromatography
bullets: In partition chromatography substances separate according to the size of their radicals, the presence of hydrophilic groups and their different solubility in the mobile and stationary solutions.

In paper chromatography the substance is spotted 1 cm above the lower edge of the strip, and the strip is placed in a chamber with a mobile (often organic) solution; for each stained substance an individual Rf is measured or the substance is identified against a standard.

slides.title: Optical methods: colorimetry, photometry, spectrophotometry
bullets: In colorimetry the substance being measured forms a coloured compound with another substance; the intensity of the solution’s colour is directly proportional to the amount of substance and is compared with the colour of a standard solution.

The stronger the colour, the higher the optical density; on the graph concentration goes on the abscissa and optical density on the ordinate; the method needs a proportional relation between optical density and concentration.
In spectrophotometry one finds at which wavelength a substance in solution or in a solid medium absorbs light.

A photometer is an optical instrument that measures light flux at fixed wavelengths: light source → entrance slit → filter passing a narrow part of the spectrum → cuvette with the sample → exit slit → detector and microprocessor.

slides.title: Optical methods: colorimetry, photometry, spectrophotometry
bullets: The photometric method is more objective than colorimetry, needs relatively simple instruments and is highly sensitive.
Most biochemical methods are measured in a cuvette with a 1 cm light path; if the optical density is 1, only 10% of the light passes and 90% is absorbed.

slides.title: Physicochemical and chemical methods (chromatography, spectro-, photometry, densitometry, etc.)?
bullets: 1. Chromatography: distribution between a mobile and a stationary phase; by mechanism – adsorption, partition, ion exchange, gel filtration, affinity; by technique – paper, thin layer, column, gas, high-performance liquid (HPLC), LC-MS/MS.
2. Clinical use: HbA1c and hemoglobin variants (ion-exchange HPLC), steroids and drug monitoring (LC-MS/MS), toxicology (GC-MS), newborn screening.
3. Spectrophotometry/photometry: absorption of monochromatic light is proportional to concentration (Beer–Lambert law); "blank" and calibrator; end-point and kinetic measurement (enzymes).
4. Other optical methods: turbidimetry, nephelometry, fluorimetry; densitometry – quantification of electrophoresis fractions.
5. Electrochemical methods: ion-selective electrodes (Na, K, Cl), gas analyzers.
